articles.title: Assist plays music from a chosen household account
articles.dek: A voice assistant can act as a selected person and use their linked streaming account.
body: Home Assistant lets an Assist voice assistant act as a chosen user. A request from a voice satellite previously carried no user identity, leaving integrations unable to choose that person’s linked account. Music Assistant can use the new setting to play from their own streaming account.

The “Acts as user” choice belongs to the assistant’s configuration; it does not recognize who is speaking. Requests from a signed-in non-administrator keep that person’s own identity, and a removed or inactive account is not adopted.
Felix Schneider supplies the implementation, settings picker and guide. The picker is his first contribution to the Home Assistant frontend.

pullRequests.title: Add user_id to assist pipelines
Add a user picker to an assist pipeline
Document the user an assist pipeline acts as

articles.title: Music Assistant gives each listener personal favourites and dislikes
articles.dek: Hearts belong to individual accounts, and disliked tracks, albums and artists stay out of automatically chosen music.
body: Music Assistant gives each household member their own favourites and dislikes. The heart shown in the interface reflects the signed-in listener’s choice, and an update from another person no longer replaces it. This extends the account protections reported on September 27, which left the app’s own hearts shared.

Personal dislikes also shape radio, mixes and autoplay: Music Assistant skips disliked tracks and music from disliked albums or artists when it chooses what to play. A track someone deliberately selects can still play. Disliking a new track does not add it to the connected music service’s library.

Marcel van der Veldt preserves existing favourites for the owners of the music sources that hold them, or for everyone when the source is shared by the whole home. Choices made on another device update the interface without a reload.

articles.title: Home Assistant protects app sign-ins from intercepted codes
articles.dek: An optional proof check ties a login code to the app that requested it, including during account linking.
body: Home Assistant completes a sign-in protection for apps that request it: a captured authorization code cannot be exchanged without the secret held by the client that began the login. The browser login flow carries the client’s proof request through to Home Assistant’s authentication service.

Allen Porter also closes an alternate route that could accept a protected code for account linking without that proof. The protection, called PKCE, applies to clients using the new flow; existing sign-ins that do not request it keep their previous behavior.

pullRequests.title: Support PKCE S256 in OAuth server

Reject PKCE authorization codes in LinkUserView

articles.title: Music Assistant plays through Teufel Raumfeld multiroom systems
articles.dek: An experimental connection exposes rooms as players and controls the system’s own speaker groups.
body: Music Assistant adds an experimental connection to Teufel Raumfeld multiroom systems. Each room appears as a player, and grouping those players creates or changes the corresponding zone on the Raumfeld host. Playback, volume and mute controls are included, along with line-in selection where a room’s device supports it.

The default continuous-stream mode supports gapless playback and crossfades across grouped rooms. In that mode, the Raumfeld app follows the track title but its clock runs across the whole queue; Music Assistant keeps the correct progress. Turning the mode off restores the Raumfeld app’s per-track clock at the cost of short gaps.
Contributor Simanias tested setup, playback and grouping on a real four-room system. This is their first contribution to the Music Assistant server, reviewed by OzGav.

pullRequests.title: Add Teufel Raumfeld player provider

articles.title: ESPHome stops visual forms overwriting hand-edited configurations
articles.dek: Moving between YAML and the visual editor no longer restores deleted values or changes the wrong row.
body: ESPHome Device Builder protects changes made directly in YAML when someone returns to its visual forms. Editing a form within a second of changing the text could previously replace the new text with older values. The forms read the current configuration before writing, while automation editors briefly pause until their updated contents are ready.

J. Nick Koston also prevents deleted formulas from being written into another action, filter or light-effect row. Moving or deleting a row could transfer its remembered values to the wrong place; entries the visual editor could not display could also make it change the wrong item or reorder the remaining entries.

When two items share the same editing address, Device Builder refuses an ambiguous change instead of silently replacing or deleting the wrong item. Its message asks the maker to give the items distinct identifiers in YAML.

articles.title: Music Assistant links the same albums across music services
articles.dek: MusicBrainz links and recording identifiers improve matching without relying on title searches alone.
body: Music Assistant uses the open MusicBrainz catalogue to connect albums and tracks in a library with the same music on other configured services. Links already recorded by MusicBrainz come before a text search; recording identifiers and album barcodes provide another way to find a match.

Marcel van der Veldt applies the matching to new or refreshed library items and gradually works through existing collections in the background. Adding another music service also links items MusicBrainz has already identified. Missing album information can be filled in without replacing details already present.
An advanced setting, enabled by default, controls linking to other music services. Linking an item does not by itself add it to that service’s library.

articles.title: UniFi Protect camera events work with API-key-only connections
articles.dek: Motion, sound, smart detection and package events no longer require the additional local account.
body: Home Assistant adds UniFi Protect camera events to connections that use only an API key. Motion, sound detection, smart detection and package events become available where the camera exposes them, broadening the existing connection’s use in automations.

Raphael Hehl verified 33 event entities on a live console that previously had none in this mode. Doorbell rings, NFC, fingerprint and vehicle events still require full access through the private interface.

articles.title: ESPHome updates compatible Nordic devices over Bluetooth
articles.dek: Device Builder and ESPHome Web add wireless updates for nRF52 devices already configured to receive them.
body: ESPHome Device Builder adds Bluetooth firmware updates for compatible nRF52 devices, alongside a serial update option. A device must already run firmware configured for the MCUboot update service. This extends the browser-based USB installation reported on September 25 with a wireless update path.

Contributor tomaszduda23 supplies the dashboard update engine, with J. Nick Koston reviewing and extending it to ESPHome Web. The standalone site accepts an app_update.bin file and checks it before offering Bluetooth or serial transfer. Bluetooth requires a browser that supports Web Bluetooth.

The work was tested on an Adafruit ItsyBitsy nRF52840 over both connections. Bluetooth discovery uses the update service advertised by the board, avoiding a remembered old device name that could keep it out of the chooser.

articles.title: Deleted Home Assistant timers stop triggering automations
articles.dek: Removing a running timer also cancels the completion event it had already scheduled.
body: Deleting a running Home Assistant timer stops its planned completion event. Previously, the deleted timer could still announce that it had finished at the original deadline and trigger automations, even though it no longer existed. Franck Nijhof cancels that pending event when the timer is removed.

pullRequests.title: Cancel running timer when the timer entity is removed

articles.title: Music Assistant reconnects radio streams before playback gives up
articles.dek: A silent connection gets a fresh attempt after ten seconds instead of waiting five minutes.
body: Music Assistant gives an internet-radio station a chance to recover when it stops sending audio but leaves the connection open. It retries that connection after ten seconds, ahead of the twenty-second silence limit that stops playback.
Previously, the connection could wait five minutes before retrying, so playback always stopped first. OzGav corrects both radio stream readers, with review by Fabian Munkes.

pullRequests.title: Reconnect radio streams that go silent before playback gives up

articles.title: ESPHome cuts the download and wait for first Nordic builds
articles.dek: Fetching only the tools a configuration needs reduces setup time and disk use; interrupted downloads can resume.
body: ESPHome reduces the download and wait for a first nRF52 firmware build by fetching only the parts of the Nordic software kit that the configuration needs. Interrupted downloads can resume instead of starting again, and the log shows their progress.

In J. Nick Koston’s test of a basic ItsyBitsy configuration, setup and the first build took 99 seconds instead of 372, with the kit using 964 MB rather than 2.2 GB. The test started with an empty kit directory but an installed Python environment and compiler; both builds produced identical firmware. Authors of external components needing extra Nordic projects must declare them explicitly.

articles.title: ESPHome adds a saved counter for pulses and sensor events
articles.dek: Makers can accumulate a total and restore its saved value after a restart.
body: ESPHome adds a counter sensor for accumulating events such as pulses from a liquid-flow sensor. It can count each update from another sensor or each on transition from a binary sensor, and restores its saved total after a restart by default.

Clyde Stubbs also supplies actions to set the count or adjust it by a chosen amount. Counting sensor updates counts the events themselves, rather than adding the measurement values. J. Nick Koston reviewed the addition.
